Understanding Retrieval-Augmented Generation

A practical guide to grounding language models in your own data

Priya Raman Mar 14, 2025

Large language models are remarkably fluent, but they do not know what they were never taught. Retrieval-Augmented Generation, usually shortened to RAG, is a technique that gives a model access to external documents at the moment a question is asked. Instead of relying only on what the model memorized during training, the system first looks up relevant passages and then asks the model to answer using them.1

Why retrieval matters

A model has a fixed knowledge cutoff and a limited context window. When you ask about a company policy written last week, the model has no way to know it. Retrieval solves this by fetching the policy text and placing it in the prompt. The answer is then grounded in a document you can inspect, which also makes it easier to check for mistakes.

There are three main benefits of this approach:

  • Answers can cite the passages they were based on.
  • Knowledge can be updated by changing the document store, without retraining.
    • New documents are searchable as soon as they are indexed.
  • Private data stays in your own infrastructure.

How the pipeline works

A basic RAG system has four steps, and the order matters because each stage feeds the next one:

  1. Split the documents into chunks of a few hundred words.
  2. Convert each chunk into an embedding, a list of numbers that captures its meaning.
  3. At question time, embed the question and find the closest chunks by cosine similarity.
  4. Insert the best chunks into the prompt and ask the model to answer from them.

A minimal example

The following Python sketch shows the retrieval step using plain lists. It is deliberately simple and is not meant for production use.

def retrieve(question_vec, chunks, k=3):
    scored = [(cosine(question_vec, c.vec), c) for c in chunks]
    scored.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0], reverse=True)
    return [c for _, c in scored[:k]]

Choosing a chunk size

Chunk size is a trade-off. Small chunks are precise but lose surrounding context, while large chunks keep context but dilute the signal. The table below summarizes the usual guidance.

Chunk sizeStrengthWeakness
Small (100 words)Precise matchesLoses context
Medium (300 words)BalancedNeeds tuning
Large (800 words)Rich contextNoisy retrieval

Common failure modes

Retrieval can fail silently. If the right passage is never retrieved, the model will often produce a confident but unsupported answer. Evaluating retrieval separately from generation helps you find out which half of the system is at fault.

Measure retrieval quality before you tune the prompt.

In practice, teams add a re-ranking step, keep a small set of test questions, and review failures by hand every week. None of this is glamorous, but it is what separates a demo from a dependable tool.

Conclusion

RAG does not make a model smarter. It makes the model better informed at the moment it answers. If you remember one idea from this article, let it be this: the quality of the answer is limited by the quality of the passages you retrieve.

1

The technique was popularized in a 2020 research paper from Facebook AI Research.
